si_note: Wording drafted with SI assistance (Claude); numbers computed from NASA PSI records; reviewed by team.

cards.title: Earth screening tests and microgravity can disagree
cards.text: In SAFFIRE-II, 4 of 4 silicone sheets showed about 0 cm of burning in microgravity at 20 cm/s airflow, yet 2 of them burned completely in the matching normal-gravity tests. The cotton-fiberglass sheet (2-5) burned its full 29 cm in microgravity.
cards.so_what: Material screening done on Earth does not map one-to-one onto flammability in a spacecraft; the direction of the difference depends on the material. NASA notes that its materials standard (NASA-STD-6001) relies on a 1-g flame test that some researchers believe is not conservative in low gravity; its SoFIE and FLARE experiments study this question.
cards.caveat: 9 samples; O2 about 21.5-22.1% (derived by NASA from CO2 production).

related.label: NASA Glenn: SoFIE, FLARE and NASA-STD-6001

cards.title: Gas flames light readily in a Moon-base atmosphere
cards.text: ACME CFI-G ran 20 tests at 7.35 psi and 33-39% O2, inside the Moon-base range given in the challenge brief. 17 of 20 lit a hot flame, which burned for up to 274 s; 13 went out on their own.
cards.so_what: At these conditions ignition is easy, so controlling ignition sources matters more than in today's cabins.
cards.caveat: Gaseous fuels on a spherical burner, not cabin materials; fuel flow rates varied.

cards.title: No cabin material has been burned at Moon-base conditions
cards.text: The solid-material tests stop near normal air: BASS-II reaches 22.2% O2 and SAFFIRE-II 22.1% O2. None of the 7 datasets burned a fabric or plastic at 30% O2 or more and 10.2 psi or less.
cards.so_what: Flammability limits for cabin materials in a Moon-base atmosphere are still unmeasured. NASA's FM2 experiment, the first combustion experiment planned on another planetary body, will burn materials at the Moon's 1/6 gravity; the challenge brief also names LUCI.
cards.caveat: Covers the 7 PSI datasets used here.

related.label: NASA Glenn: Flammability of Materials on the Moon (FM2)

cards.title: Smoke tests cover still air and long aging
cards.text: SAME-R logged 109 smoke records from 5 heated cabin materials (Kapton, Teflon, silicone, lampwick, Pyrell). 22 were made in still air (0 cm/s) and the rest at up to 8.1 cm/s; smoke was aged for up to 1923 s before measurement.
cards.so_what: Detector design can draw on smoke that drifts slowly and ages in still air, as it would in a poorly ventilated corner of a habitat.
cards.caveat: Test conditions only; particle-size results are in the SAME-R reports.

cards.title: Smoke particle sizes are not in the data table
cards.text: None of the 109 SAME-R records in the PSI experimental table carry particle-size results.
cards.so_what: Detector thresholds need the measured sizes; they must be taken from the SAME-R reports.
cards.caveat: Science lead to add the report values.

cards.title: Lowering oxygen puts droplet fires out
cards.text: In FLEX, droplet flames in normal air (21% O2, about 1 atm) went out before the fuel was used up in 14 of 29 tests. At 16% O2 or less that rose to 33 of 36.
cards.so_what: Lowering the oxygen share extinguishes these flames; FLEX tested the same idea with CO2 and helium as suppressants.
cards.caveat: Methanol and heptane droplets, nitrogen dilution only; not cabin solids.

cards.title: High-oxygen fires rarely go out on their own
cards.text: At 30-34% O2, only 2 of 24 FLEX droplet flames went out on their own; 18 ended with the droplet breaking apart. In the 17 tests closest to Moon-base pressure (about 10.3-10.4 psi), 0 went out on their own.
cards.so_what: In a 30%+ O2 habitat, suppression systems cannot count on fires dying out; they must act.
cards.caveat: Liquid droplets; 'disruption' = the droplet broke up, ending the test.

cards.title: Fabric and acrylic kept burning in thinned microgravity air
cards.text: In BASS-II microgravity tests, 27 of 27 cotton-fiberglass (SIBAL) strips logged no extinction or blowoff at 16.4-20.8% O2, 14 of them below 18% O2. Below 16% O2, 8 of 16 acrylic (PMMA) rod runs logged no extinction, down to 14.2% O2; the only failed ignition was at 13.6% O2.
cards.so_what: In microgravity a fabric or plastic fire can keep going in air well below the cabin's ~21% O2, so modestly lowering cabin oxygen should not be counted on to stop a solid-material fire.
cards.caveat: BASS-II (ISS glovebox, cabin pressure not reported). 'No extinction logged' (outcome burned_or_not_stated) means the test log notes no flame-out; it does not confirm a full burn. Airflow varied run to run and is given only as raw fan/air settings; 27 fabric strips, 16 low-O2 rod runs of three diameters (the rest went out, blew off or did not ignite).
cards.question: Q1
cards.question_text: Will the material burn, and how far will the flame spread?

cards.title: Where samples burned in orbit, 1g spread sped up
cards.text: Of the 5 SAFFIRE-II samples that kept burning in microgravity, 4 burned completely in the matching normal-gravity test, 4 with flame spread that kept speeding up. In microgravity, only 2 reached the end of the sample, each with a single measured spread rate; the other 3 burned only part-way.
cards.so_what: For materials that do burn in orbit, a 1g test can show more aggressive, accelerating spread than microgravity at the same airflow; with card P1 (the reverse for silicone), this means 1g results need a microgravity check before being used to judge how far a fire could spread.
cards.caveat: 9 SAFFIRE-II sheets at about 22% O2 and 20 cm/s flow, mostly concurrent; 5 burned in microgravity. Two of them (2-6, 2-9) have no fuel named in the table; 2-7 was PMMA paired with Nomex and 2-8 thick PMMA. The part-way burn lengths carry table notes not in this dataset (possibly test-time limits). Burn lengths and 1g results are table text, not numeric fields.
cards.question: Q1
cards.question_text: Will the material burn, and how far will the flame spread?

cards.title: Oxygen-rich air keeps gas flames burning far longer
cards.text: In ACME CFI-G normal-flame tests at 20.7-21.7% cabin O2, 37 of 37 hot flames went out on their own, the longest after 20 s. At 33-40% O2, 58 of 61 self-extinguishing flames outlasted that (up to 304 s), and 30 more were still burning when the fuel flow was cut.
cards.so_what: In an oxygen-enriched habitat, a small fire may not burn itself out as quickly as it tends to in ISS-like air, so detection and response windows sized from normal-air experience may be too short.
cards.caveat: Gaseous fuels (ethane, propane, butane, pure and diluted) on a spherical porous burner in quiescent microgravity, not cabin materials. Fuel flow rates and pressures (about 7.35-44 psi) varied; the gap also appears at each pressure tested in both bands and among tests with matching fuel flow, but these were not controlled pairings. Flames ended by cutting the fuel flow (some at the burner temperature limit) have burn times that are lower bounds.
cards.question: Q2
cards.question_text: How does oxygen-rich air change the risk?

cards.title: In cabin-oxygen tests, cool flames came only at high O2
cards.text: In ACME CFI-G normal-flame tests, 7 butane-mixture flames showed cool flames alongside hot burning at 29.4 psi and 38.9-39.9% O2. At 7.35 psi and about 35% O2, 2 more lit only as a cool flame. Of 11 butane-mixture tests near 21% O2, 0% reported a cool flame.
cards.so_what: Cool flames burn at low temperature with little visible light, so in an oxygen-rich, low-pressure habitat a fuel leak could react without the bright flame that crews and optical sensors expect; detector and ignition-control design for Moon-base air should consider them.
cards.caveat: Butane diluted to 30% or 50% in inert gas on a spherical porous burner; 9 tests in total, from a few test days. Cool flames were flagged by the investigators in the table; their absence near 21% O2 covers only 11 butane tests and does not show they cannot occur there. Propane and ethane tests reported none in normal-flame mode.
cards.question: Q2
cards.question_text: How does oxygen-rich air change the risk?

cards.title: High-oxygen gas flames are calculated to burn hotter
cards.text: For ACME CFI-G normal flames that lit at 20.7-21.7% cabin O2, the data table's calculated adiabatic flame temperature reached at most 2276 K. At 33-40% O2, 86 of 91 lit flames were calculated hotter than that, up to 2730 K.
cards.so_what: A hotter flame radiates and conducts more heat to nearby surfaces, so in Moon-base air a small fire could heat and ignite neighbouring materials faster than ISS experience suggests; spacing and thermal-protection margins should allow for it.
cards.caveat: Tad is a calculated value from the gas mixture, not a measured flame temperature. Gaseous fuels (ethane, propane, butane, pure and diluted) on a spherical porous burner in microgravity; pressures (about 7.35-44 psi) and fuel dilution varied and were not paired by design, though the gap shows at each pressure tested in both bands except a few low-Tad 30% butane tests at 14.7 psi.
cards.question: Q2
cards.question_text: How does oxygen-rich air change the risk?

cards.title: Near 21% O2, low pressure did not stop gas flames
cards.text: In ACME CFI-G normal-flame tests at 20.7-21.7% O2, 3 of 5 flames at 7.35 psi lit hot and each burned 14-20 s before going out. At 29.39-44.09 psi, 15 of 24 lit, but none lasted beyond 7 s. At 33-40% O2 the gap closed: the longest self-extinguishing flames burned 258 s at 7.35 psi and 251 s at 29.39 psi.
cards.so_what: Lowering cabin pressure did not stop gas flames from lighting in cabin-like air, and the low-pressure flames lasted longer, so a reduced-pressure habitat should not count on thin air to shorten a fire.
cards.caveat: Gaseous fuels on a spherical burner, not cabin materials. Near 21% O2 the 7.35 psi tests used only 50% butane (5 tests, two noted the igniter lingered in the flame) and the 29-44 psi tests only 30% propane (24 tests); fuel flow rate varied and is not matched, so fuel and pressure are confounded.
cards.question: Q3
cards.question_text: What happens at lower pressure and partial gravity?

cards.title: No partial-gravity tests; low-pressure data are gas only
cards.text: None of the 1018 records in the 7 datasets was run at Moon (1/6 g) or Mars (3/8 g) gravity; the only non-microgravity results are 9 SAFFIRE-II Earth-gravity comparisons. At 10.2 psi or less there are 65 prevention records, all ACME CFI-G gas flames (25 normal, 40 inverse). Of 259 solid-material records, 0 report any pressure.
cards.so_what: Partial gravity brings back weak buoyant flow that neither microgravity nor Earth tests reproduce, and low-pressure evidence covers only burner gas flames, so Moon and Mars habitat materials have no direct test basis here.
cards.caveat: Absence within these 7 PSI datasets only; inverse-flame (I-) records give burner-stream O2, not cabin air. Solid tests (BASS, BASS-II, SAFFIRE-II) report no pressure; BASS-II assumes about 1 atm cabin.
cards.question: Q3
cards.question_text: What happens at lower pressure and partial gravity?

cards.title: Solid-fuel emulator data cannot separate oxygen effects
cards.text: ACME BRE, a gas burner that emulates burning solids, logged 43 day-level records over 18 test days at 21-40% O2, 23 of them at 30% O2 or more. Ignitions are given only as one total per day across several O2 levels, and 43 of 43 records give no pressure.
cards.so_what: BRE is the PSI dataset closest to a burning solid at Moon-base oxygen levels, but the published table cannot show how ignition changes from 21% to 40% O2 or with pressure; per-test results would be needed to use it for habitat material limits.
cards.caveat: Ethylene (pure or 50% in nitrogen) and methane on 25 mm and 50 mm porous burners. O2 values are approximate levels for the tests that ignited that day. Only the PSI experimental table was examined, not the investigators' papers.
cards.question: Q4
cards.question_text: Where are the gaps?

cards.title: Burning-solid tests give no pressure and one airflow
cards.text: Of 138 BASS-II and SAFFIRE-II solid-material records, 0 report a chamber pressure, so no burning plastic or fabric is tied to a reduced habitat pressure. All 9 SAFFIRE-II sheets ran at a single airflow (20 cm/s), only 1 with the flame spreading against the air; BASS-II gives airflow speed in cm/s for 0 of 129 records.
cards.so_what: Moon-base cabins are planned at 10.2 psi or less and with weak, varied ventilation, yet the real-material data cannot show how pressure or airflow speed changes flame spread; a solid-material series across pressure and at least two flow speeds in each direction would fill this.
cards.caveat: BASS-II (mostly PMMA and SIBAL fabric) and SAFFIRE-II (9 sheets incl. silicone, SIBAL, PMMA/Nomex). Pressure may be recorded in the investigators' papers; only the PSI experimental table was examined. BASS-II airflow is given as raw controller settings, not converted to cm/s.
cards.question: Q4
cards.question_text: Where are the gaps?

cards.title: Every material got the same smoke-generation time
cards.text: In SAME-R, 67 of 68 records with a reported smoke-generation time heated the sample for 60 s, across 5 of 5 materials. The exception is 1 Kapton still-air run at 120 s. Another 41 records, 41 of them aged-smoke measurements, leave duration blank.
cards.so_what: Because heating time was held fixed, a detector designer can compare smoke samples across the five materials without a duration difference getting in the way; heater setting and airflow are the variables left to watch.
cards.caveat: SAME-R (PSI-101) only, 109 records from 5 heated cabin materials in ISS cabin air; this table lists sampling conditions, not particle sizes, so it shows how smoke was produced, not what it looked like. Heater settings were not matched across materials (see D-A2).
cards.question: Q1
cards.question_text: What does smoke from each material look like?

cards.title: Kapton has the most smoke samples, Teflon the fewest
cards.text: Per material, SAME-R sampled Kapton most: 29 records, 13 of them aged-smoke measurements. Teflon has the fewest: 18 records, 6 aged, at 3 airflow levels (still air, low flow and 8.1 cm/s). Heater settings also vary unevenly: Silicone, Lampwick and Teflon used 5, 5 and 5 settings, Pyrell only 3.
cards.so_what: A smoke-detector designer has the most samples for Kapton wiring insulation and the fewest for Teflon, so per-material detector tuning for Teflon or Pyrell smoke rests on fewer or less varied samples.
cards.caveat: SAME-R (PSI-101) only, 18-29 records per material in ISS cabin air; one Teflon record (test 57) shares its test number and values with a Lampwick record. Particle-size results are not in the table, so this describes what was sampled, not the smoke itself.
cards.question: Q1
cards.question_text: What does smoke from each material look like?

cards.title: Heater settings differ from material to material
cards.text: SAME-R did not use one shared heater setting (resistance ratio) across materials. Pyrell ran at 1.22-1.23, silicone at 1.304-1.36 and Kapton at 1.38-1.48, so these three ranges do not overlap.
cards.so_what: Differences in smoke between these materials are tied up with differences in heater setting, so the matrix alone cannot separate the effect of material from the effect of heating level.
cards.caveat: Heater setting is the ratio Rt/R0 as tabulated; its link to sample temperature is not given in the table. Lampwick and Teflon not shown; Teflon includes one low-setting outlier.
cards.question: Q2
cards.question_text: How do heating level and airflow change the smoke?

cards.title: Heater level was varied mainly in the fastest airflow
cards.text: Within a material, SAME-R changed the heater setting mostly at 8.1 cm/s. Kapton ran at 4 heater settings there but 1 in still air; silicone 4 versus 1; Teflon 5 versus 1. So heating level can be compared within these materials only in the fastest flow, and airflow mainly at one fixed heater setting.
cards.so_what: A detector designer can study heating level and airflow separately for these materials, but not together: in still air each was run at a single heater setting, so how heating changes still-air smoke cannot be seen.
cards.caveat: SAME-R only (PSI-101), ISS cabin air; Kapton, silicone and Teflon shown (Pyrell and Lampwick ran two settings in still air). Heater setting is the tabulated ratio Rt/R0; record counts per cell are small and smoke particle sizes are not in the table.
cards.question: Q2
cards.question_text: How do heating level and airflow change the smoke?

cards.title: Long-aged smoke sampled in still air for every material
cards.text: 44 SAME-R records aged smoke for 557 s or more before measurement. 10 of them were in still air, covering 5 of 5 materials, and 3 were at 1 cm/s.
cards.so_what: Smoke that lingers for many minutes in a poorly ventilated module can change before it reaches a detector; SAME-R has such aged samples in still air for each material, which detector designers can draw on via the SAME-R reports.
cards.caveat: Aging times are test conditions; how the smoke changed with aging is in the SAME-R reports, not this table. Five materials; few long-aged records per material.
cards.question: Q3
cards.question_text: How does smoke change as it ages and travels?

cards.title: Fresh smoke and re-measured aged smoke sampled separately
cards.text: Most SAME-R smoke was measured fresh: 58 of 63 normal samples with an aging time had aged 21-62 s, including 8 s of mixing. 42 aged-measurement records, across 5 materials, re-measured smoke at 218-1923 s. Separately, 5 normal samples from 5 materials were held 720 s before mixing, 5 of them at 8.1 cm/s.
cards.so_what: A detector at the far end of a still module sees smoke minutes old, not the seconds-old smoke most samples captured; SAME-R's aged re-measurements and long-hold runs are the records to use when tuning for drifted smoke.
cards.caveat: Aging times are test conditions; how particles changed is in the SAME-R reports, not this table. Five materials, ISS cabin air; the long primary holds were one run per material at the highest flow only, and one aged record has no aging time.
cards.question: Q3
cards.question_text: How does smoke change as it ages and travels?

cards.title: Low-airflow smoke tests are thinly sampled
cards.text: Only 11 of 109 SAME-R records were made at 1-2 cm/s airflow, against 76 at 8 cm/s or more. Lampwick and Teflon have 0 records at 1 cm/s, and the 5 records at 2 cm/s include 0 aged-smoke measurements.
cards.so_what: Habitat air often moves slowly, yet most of the SAME-R matrix sits at the fastest flow; detector responses to slow-drifting smoke rest on few samples, and some material and flow combinations are missing.
cards.caveat: Five heated cabin materials on ISS; counts are test conditions from the PSI table, not smoke measurements. Flow is SAME-R inlet velocity.
cards.question: Q4
cards.question_text: Where are the gaps?

cards.title: No smoke data for oxygen-rich, low-pressure air
cards.text: Of 109 SAME-R smoke records, 0 report an oxygen level and 0 report a pressure; 109 are logged as ISS cabin air. So there are 0 smoke records for Moon-base air (30% O2 or more, 10.2 psi or less), and none of the 5 heated materials has a smoke sample outside normal cabin air.
cards.so_what: Smoke detectors for a Moon base would be tuned on smoke made only in ISS cabin air; a SAME-R-style run at raised O2 and reduced pressure is the missing test before trusting those thresholds there.
cards.caveat: Five heated cabin materials, 109 records, all on ISS; oxygen and pressure are not in the PSI table and are assumed to be normal cabin air. Absence in the table does not rule out unpublished tests.
cards.question: Q4
cards.question_text: Where are the gaps?

cards.title: Adding CO2 to air: more heptane flames went out
cards.text: At 17-21% O2 and about 1 atm, FLEX heptane droplet flames went out before the fuel was used up in 12 of 18 tests with CO2 added, 5 of 11 with helium added, and 7 of 20 with nitrogen only. Methanol flames went out in 17 of 19 CO2 tests and 7 of 7 helium tests.
cards.so_what: At the same oxygen level, swapping some nitrogen for CO2 went with more heptane flames going out, which is consistent with CO2 as an extinguishing agent; for methanol nearly every diluted flame went out either way.
cards.caveat: Single droplets of heptane and methanol, not cabin solids; small samples (7-20 per group); the added CO2 or helium share (5-20%) was not matched test by test, and no significance test was run.
cards.question: Q1
cards.question_text: What puts the flame out?

cards.title: More CO2 added, more flames went out
cards.text: In FLEX at 10.3-10.4 psi and 23-25% O2, droplet flames went out before the fuel was used up more often with more CO2 added. At a CO2 fraction of 0.15-0.2: heptane 2 of 7, methanol 3 of 10. At 0.25 (all at 23% O2): heptane 3 of 4, methanol 6 of 8.
cards.so_what: At a reduced cabin pressure close to planned exploration habitats, a modest step up in CO2 went with most droplet flames going out in both fuels, which is the kind of dose information a CO2 or inert-gas suppression design needs.
cards.caveat: Single heptane and methanol droplets, not cabin solids; small groups (4-10 tests); oxygen was not held exactly fixed (the higher-CO2 tests sat at the low end of the O2 band), droplet size varied, and most low-CO2 flames that did not go out broke apart instead. No significance test.
cards.question: Q1
cards.question_text: What puts the flame out?

cards.title: Heptane flames often went out with fuel left
cards.text: In FLEX at about 1 atm, for droplets starting 3-4 mm across whose flames went out, 14 of 17 heptane droplets were still at least 2.5 mm across when the flame died, versus 12 of 24 methanol droplets.
cards.so_what: A flame going out does not mean the fuel is gone: most heptane droplets here still held liquid that could evaporate or re-ignite, so re-ignition checks after suppression matter.
cards.caveat: Single liquid droplets, not cabin solids; groups pool CO2, helium and nitrogen-only tests across 12-30% O2 and were not matched on diluent or oxygen; extinction diameter is the visible-flame estimate and is missing for some tests. No significance test.
cards.question: Q1
cards.question_text: What puts the flame out?

cards.title: Diluted heptane flames went out more at lower pressure
cards.text: With CO2 or helium added at 17-21% O2, FLEX heptane droplet flames went out before burnout in 15 of 16 tests at about 10.4 psi, versus 17 of 29 at about 1 atm. Methanol showed no such gap: 24 of 26 versus 24 of 26.
cards.so_what: Lower cabin pressure at the same oxygen percentage went with more heptane flames going out, but habitats that lower pressure usually raise the oxygen percentage, which pushes the other way (see S2).
cards.caveat: Same O2 mole fraction means less oxygen per volume at the lower pressure, so pressure and oxygen partial pressure are not separated. Single fuel droplets, not cabin solids; 16 vs 29 heptane tests; diluent share (5-20%) not matched.
cards.question: Q2
cards.question_text: How do oxygen-rich air, fuel and pressure change that?

cards.title: Heptane flames went out less often than methanol
cards.text: In FLEX nitrogen-only air at 18-21% O2 and about 1 atm, methanol droplet flames went out before the fuel was used up in 13 of 16 tests, but heptane flames did so in only 7 of 20; the rest of the heptane droplets burned out or broke apart.
cards.so_what: How readily a fire goes out depends strongly on the fuel: oxygen levels that stopped most methanol flames stopped far fewer heptane flames, so suppression margins should be set by the hardest-to-extinguish fuel aboard.
cards.caveat: Single liquid droplets in quiescent microgravity, not cabin solids; 16 methanol and 20 heptane tests; droplet sizes not matched; O2 levels within the band not evenly split between fuels.
cards.question: Q2
cards.question_text: How do oxygen-rich air, fuel and pressure change that?

cards.title: BASS-II: airflow blowoff recorded only in thinned oxygen
cards.text: BASS-II recorded 24 acrylic (PMMA) flames that went out in microgravity. 7 were blown off by the airflow, all at 15-17.4% O2. The other 17 went out at 14.8-20.9% O2, including 6 in near-normal air (20% O2 or more).
cards.so_what: Acrylic flames sometimes went out on their own even in near-normal air, while blowing a flame off with airflow was only recorded once oxygen was already lowered; the data give no support for relying on airflow alone to put out a cabin fire.
cards.caveat: PMMA only; 104 of 129 BASS-II records do not state an outcome, so rates cannot be computed; air-flow settings are raw controller units; high airflow was not tested evenly across O2 levels.
cards.question: Q3
cards.question_text: Can airflow or venting put a fire out?

cards.title: No airflow speed measured in any suppression test
cards.text: None of these suppression tests gives airflow as a speed. 274 of 274 FLEX droplet tests report no flow (droplets burned in still air). 129 of 129 BASS-II records give airflow only as raw controller settings, and 3 of the 7 BASS-II blowoffs have no air setting recorded at all.
cards.so_what: There is no measured airflow speed at which a flame was blown out, so these data cannot tell a habitat engineer how hard ventilation would need to blow, or whether venting would help or feed a fire.
cards.caveat: FLEX is liquid droplets (methanol, heptane) in quiescent air; BASS-II is mostly PMMA, with raw air settings that are not convertible to cm/s and several logged as a range (e.g. lowered until extinction); SAFFIRE-II (20 cm/s) is outside this pillar.
cards.question: Q3
cards.question_text: Can airflow or venting put a fire out?

cards.title: No added suppressant tested in Moon-base air
cards.text: Of 274 FLEX droplet tests, 17 ran in Moon-base-like air (30% O2 or more, about 10.5 psi or less), and 0 of those had CO2 or helium added; all 17 used nitrogen only. Tests with an added agent stop at 25% O2 for CO2 (123 tests) and 24% O2 for helium (50 tests).
cards.so_what: A CO2 extinguisher discharged into a Moon-base cabin would be acting on oxygen-rich, low-pressure air that no FLEX run combined with an added agent; that pairing is a clear first target for a new suppression experiment.
cards.caveat: Liquid droplets only (methanol and heptane) in quiescent microgravity; 'Moon-base-like' uses a 10.5 psi cutoff because FLEX low-pressure runs sit at about 10.2-10.5 psi; FLEX diluent is pre-mixed in the chamber, not discharged onto a fire.
cards.question: Q4
cards.question_text: Where are the gaps?

cards.title: Suppressant tests cover two liquid fuels, no cabin solids
cards.text: All 274 FLEX suppression tests burned liquid droplets of 2 fuels (methanol, heptane), using 3 gas mixes: CO2, helium or nitrogen only, with no water mist. BASS-II burned 129 solid samples (acrylic, fabric, Nomex), but 0 had CO2 or another agent added; its 24 flame-outs came from thinner oxygen or airflow alone.
cards.so_what: Cabin fires are most likely to involve plastics, fabrics and wiring insulation, yet no record here shows how CO2, helium or water mist acts on a burning solid in microgravity; such tests would turn droplet results into guidance for real habitat extinguishers.
cards.caveat: BASS-II diluent is null (not reported) for every record, read here as no agent added; BASS-II chamber CO2 measured only as a combustion product (up to about 3% at test end). FLEX droplets are a model fuel, not cabin materials; BASS (PSI-26) has no conditions or outcomes and is excluded.
cards.question: Q4
cards.question_text: Where are the gaps?

agents.rule: every number computed from tests.json filters and re-checked; hand-typed numbers, safety absolutes and duplicates rejected

prevention.headline: Oxygen-rich air kept test gas flames burning longer; cabin materials there remain untested
prevention.summary: In NASA microgravity tests, gas flames at Moon-base oxygen levels lit readily and burned far longer than in ISS-like air; lower pressure did not stop gas flames near 21% O2. Earth screening and microgravity results disagreed for some materials. No fabric or plastic has been burned at Moon-base oxygen and pressure, or in partial gravity.

key_points.text: Oxygen-rich air: in ACME gas-flame tests at 33-40% O2, flames lasted far longer before going out than in ISS-like air, so response windows sized from normal-air experience may be too short. Gas fuels only.
Will it burn: Earth screening and microgravity disagreed in a small SAFFIRE-II set, in either direction depending on the material, so 1g flammability results need a microgravity check.
Lower pressure: near 21% O2, gas flames still lit at 7.35 psi and outlasted higher-pressure flames, so thin air should not be counted on to shorten a fire. Fuel and pressure were confounded.

top_gap.text: No fabric or plastic in the 7 PSI datasets has been burned at 30% O2 or more and 10.2 psi or less, and nothing was tested at Moon or Mars gravity; low-pressure evidence is gas flames only.

next_test.text: Burn common cabin fabrics and plastics in microgravity at Moon-base conditions (30% O2 or more, 10.2 psi or less), recording pressure and using at least two airflow speeds in each direction, because no cabin material has data there.

equipment.text: Materials screening may need a microgravity check, since Earth flammability tests and orbit results disagreed for some SAFFIRE-II materials; oxygen-rich air kept gas flames burning far longer, so screening at raised O2 could be added.

earth.text: These results may inform fire safety in oxygen-enriched settings on Earth, such as medical oxygen use or hyperbaric rooms: in these microgravity tests, raised oxygen kept gas flames burning far longer than normal air.

detection.headline: Habitat smoke detectors would rest on ISS-air smoke, mostly sampled at the fastest airflow
detection.summary: SAME-R sampled smoke from 5 heated cabin materials in ISS cabin air, including long-aged smoke in still air for every material. But most records sit at the fastest flow, heater settings differ between materials, particle sizes are in the SAME-R reports, not the table, and no smoke was made in Moon-base air (30% O2 or more, 10.2 psi or less).

key_points.text: Aged smoke was sampled in still air for every material, plus re-measurements of minutes-old smoke: the records to use when tuning detectors for drifted smoke. How it changed is in the SAME-R reports.

Heating level and airflow can be studied only separately: heater level was varied mainly at the fastest flow, still-air runs used one heater setting per material, and heater settings differ between materials.
Smoke-generation time was held fixed across all 5 materials, easing comparison, but per-material detector tuning for Teflon or Pyrell rests on fewer or less varied samples than Kapton.

top_gap.text: None of the 109 SAME-R smoke records was made outside ISS cabin air, so there is no smoke data for Moon-base air (30% O2 or more, 10.2 psi or less); detector thresholds there would rest on ISS-air smoke.

next_test.text: Run a SAME-R-style smoke test at raised O2 and reduced pressure, in still air and slow flow with aged-smoke measurements and particle sizes, so Moon-base detector thresholds are tuned on matching smoke, not ISS cabin air.

equipment.text: Smoke detector alarm thresholds could be tuned on SAME-R aged smoke sampled in still air for every material, but low-airflow records are thin and no smoke was made in oxygen-rich, low-pressure air.

earth.text: SAME-R still-air and aged-smoke records are relevant to smoke detection in still-air spaces on Earth, where smoke drifts slowly, and may inform detector tuning there; they were not tested for Earth uses.

suppression.headline: Droplet fires in Moon-base-like air rarely went out alone; no suppressant tested there
suppression.summary: In FLEX droplet tests, lower oxygen or added CO2 went with more flames going out, and heptane flames went out less readily than methanol. At 30% O2 or more, few flames went out on their own. No added agent was tested in Moon-base-like air or on burning solids, and no airflow speed was measured.

key_points.text: At 30-34% O2, only 2 of 24 FLEX droplet flames went out on their own, and 0 of 17 near Moon-base pressure: in oxygen-rich habitats, suppression cannot count on fires dying out.

Adding CO2 went with more droplet flames going out, at about 1 atm and at reduced pressure. Heptane went out less readily than methanol, so the hardest fuel aboard should set the margin. Small samples.
BASS-II acrylic flames were blown off by airflow only in thinned oxygen (15-17.4% O2); with no airflow speed measured, these data give no support for relying on airflow or venting alone.

top_gap.text: No added suppressant was tested in Moon-base-like air: all 17 FLEX runs at 30% O2 or more and low pressure used nitrogen only, and no BASS-II solid sample had CO2 or another agent added.

next_test.text: Add CO2 to flames in Moon-base-like air (30% O2 or more, about 10.2 psi), first on droplets to extend FLEX, then on acrylic and fabric samples, checking for re-ignition; no run has combined an agent with that air.

equipment.text: CO2 extinguisher doses for oxygen-rich habitats need testing: more CO2 went with more droplet flames going out, yet few flames went out alone at 30% O2 or more. Heptane often left fuel; check re-ignition.

earth.text: These droplet results may inform gas-flooding suppression on Earth, such as CO2 systems, and checks for re-ignition after a fire is knocked down: heptane flames often went out with fuel left.

overall.headline: Oxygen-rich air kept test flames burning longer; no suppressant or cabin material tested there
overall.summary: In NASA microgravity tests, gas flames in oxygen-rich air lit readily and burned far longer than in ISS-like air, and droplet flames there rarely went out on their own. Yet no fabric or plastic, smoke sample or added suppressant has been tested at Moon-base oxygen and pressure, and nothing at Moon or Mars gravity.

missions.text: Planned Moon-base air (30% O2 or more, 10.2 psi or less) sits where test gas flames lit readily and droplet flames rarely went out alone, but no cabin material, smoke sample or added suppressant was tested there, and nothing at 1/6 g.

No PSI test ran at Mars gravity (3/8 g), where weak buoyant flow returns that neither microgravity nor Earth tests reproduce. Far from rescue, crews need detection and suppression evidence; here smoke came only from ISS cabin air and suppressants met only liquid droplets.

key_points.text: In oxygen-rich air, test gas flames burned far longer than in ISS-like air and droplet flames rarely went out on their own, while no added suppressant was tested at Moon-base-like conditions.

Cool flames with little visible light appeared only in high-oxygen gas tests, and normal-air response windows may be too short there, yet every smoke sample for detector tuning came from ISS cabin air.
Lowering oxygen put most test droplet flames out, but microgravity fabric and acrylic logged no flame-out in air well below 21% O2, and no suppressant was tested on a burning solid.

top_gap.text: In the 7 PSI datasets no fabric or plastic was burned, no smoke made, no added suppressant tested at Moon-base oxygen and pressure (30% O2 or more, 10.2 psi or less); no test ran at Moon or Mars gravity.

next_test.text: Burn cabin fabrics and plastics in microgravity at Moon-base air (30% O2 or more, 10.2 psi or less) at two or more airflow speeds, then discharge CO2, sampling smoke throughout, to fill each pillar's biggest gap in one series.
